Why Mid-Market Companies Are Quietly Outpacing the Fortune 500 on AI Adoption

By Reese Calder · January 31, 2024 · More from this author

The standard narrative on enterprise AI says that the biggest companies are leading the charge. The numbers tell a more interesting story. While the Fortune 500 makes the headlines, it’s mid-market firms — companies with annual revenue between $100 million and $2 billion — that are quietly running away with the productivity gains.

A 2024 BridgeWater Research survey of 1,400 IT directors found that 67 percent of mid-market firms now have at least one generative AI deployment in production, compared to just 41 percent at Fortune 500 companies. The same survey reported that mid-market AI projects deliver an average return on investment within 7 months, versus 14 months for enterprise deployments.

The reasons are not mysterious. Mid-market companies have less procurement bureaucracy, fewer legacy systems to integrate around, and tighter feedback loops between IT, the business, and the CEO’s office. “The agility gap between mid-market and enterprise AI teams is the most underappreciated story in the tech sector right now,” said Dr. Marcus Vance of the McKinsey Digital Practice at last quarter’s CIO Strategy Forum in Boston.

The spending numbers reinforce the picture. Industry analysts at Forrester now estimate that mid-market firms will spend an aggregate $34 billion on AI tools in 2025, roughly double their 2023 spend. Enterprise spend is growing too, but more slowly — in the high single digits, year over year.

Confidence is asymmetric as well. A separate poll of 200 small-to-medium business CEOs conducted last fall by The Workforce Institute showed that 78 percent expect their current AI investments to fully replace at least two existing software vendors within the next 24 months. By contrast, only 23 percent of Fortune 1000 CEOs expressed similar confidence in a parallel BridgeWater data set.

What this means for vendors is straightforward. The center of gravity in enterprise software is shifting downmarket faster than the marketing decks suggest. Vendors who built their playbooks around six-figure deals with the Fortune 100 may find that their growth comes from a different customer entirely — and that the customer doesn’t want a year-long pilot.

Whether the gap closes or widens through 2025 is the real question. Insiders we spoke to are betting on the latter.
